lessons: Lead immediately with a shocking fact or vivid contrast rather than asking rhetorical questions or stating what something is NOT (e.g., 'Shark older than US' achieved >100% end retention).
Avoid filler setup lines right after the hook; stating obvious observations like 'They are not just there to look cool' or 'They look like similar fruits' lost up to 31.5% of viewers instantly.
Do not repeat the video title or main question in the first sentence of the script; repeating the hook word-for-word caused immediate drops of 31.9%.
Never pause momentum for audience participation gimmicks like 'Pause and guess...'; these create sharp retention drops midway through.
Deliver immediate explanatory value—videos that delayed the core scientific mechanism with slow background preambles suffered massive early dropoffs.
worst_moment_types: Empty fluff or filler lines following the hook (e.g., 'They are not just there to look cool', 'They look like similar fruits')
Literal repetition of the video title or question as the opening line
Mid-video pauses or callouts asking viewers to stop and guess
Slow background setups and preambles before introducing the core topic mechanism
Negative framing hooks focusing on debunking what something is NOT rather than revealing what it IS
best_hook_types: Bold historical or scale comparisons (e.g., 'This shark is older than the United States')
Direct visual and sensory contrasts between familiar items (e.g., 'Tuna steak looks like deep red beef while cod is bright white')
Counter-intuitive everyday physical paradoxes presented as direct statements (e.g., 'You can touch hot foil briefly just as it comes out of the oven')
Intriguing mystery claims about famous scientific topics (e.g., 'Most James Webb images hold secrets')
